title: 黄瓜设施栽培关键技术
text:
Key Technologies of Protected Cucumber (*Cucumis sativus* L.) Cultivation: Technical Framework and Application Effects in Chinese Solar Greenhouses and High Tunnels
Mingyu Zhang¹, Lihua Wang²\*  
¹ College of Horticulture, Shandong Agricultural University, Tai’an 271018, Shandong, China  
² Vegetable Technology Extension Station of Shouguang City, Shouguang 262700, Shandong, China  
*Corresponding author: lihuawang@shouguang-veg.gov.cn  
Funding: This work was supported by Shandong Provincial Key R&D Program (Grant No. 2022CXGC0106)

---

 Abstract
Protected cultivation is the dominant production system for off-season cucumber supply in temperate regions, but unscientific management often causes continuous cropping obstacles, low resource use efficiency and reduced fruit quality. This study systematically constructs a whole-cycle key technical system for protected cucumber based on 2 years (2022–2023) of定位 (in-situ) trials in Chinese solar greenhouses and plastic high tunnels in North China, covering cultivar screening and grafting, precision environmental regulation, water-fertilizer integration, canopy management, and green pest control. A comparative field experiment was further conducted to verify the performance of the integrated system. Results showed that compared with conventional farmer practices, the integrated technical system increased total cucumber yield by 22.4%, premium fruit rate by 22.8%, reduced chemical pesticide input by 40.5%, irrigation water by 35.0% and chemical fertilizer by 32.1%, with a 31.0% increase in net return. This standardized technical framework provides practical guidance for high-yield, high-quality and sustainable protected cucumber production, and can be adapted to protected vegetable production regions with similar climatic conditions.
Keywords: *Cucumis sativus* L.; protected horticulture; environmental manipulation; grafting; integrated water-fertilizer management; green pest management

---

 1. Introduction
Cucumber (*Cucumis sativus* L.) is one of the most widely cultivated vegetable crops globally, with a total global production of 93.8 million tons in 2022, of which China accounts for more than 75% (FAO, 2023). As a thermophilic, heliophilous and humidity-sensitive crop, cucumber is vulnerable to low temperature, weak light and frost in open-field conditions during winter and early spring. Protected cultivation systems, including Chinese solar greenhouses, plastic high tunnels and multi-span glass greenhouses, break seasonal temperature and light limitations and realize year-round supply, with protected cucumber accounting for 62% of China’s total cucumber output in 2022 (Chinese Society of Horticultural Science, 2020).

However, smallholder-dominated protected cucumber production generally faces prominent problems: continuous monocropping causes soil salinization and soil-borne diseases; rough management of temperature, humidity and light leads to abnormal fruit development; flood irrigation and excessive fertilizer application reduce water and nutrient use efficiency; and overuse of chemical pesticides raises food safety risks. Existing studies mostly focus on a single technical measure, while systematic, production-oriented integrated technical frameworks suitable for mainstream solar greenhouse and high tunnel systems are still insufficient.

This paper summarizes a full-cycle key technical system for protected cucumber targeting high yield, premium quality and low environmental cost, and verifies its application effects through field trials in the core cucumber production region of Shouguang, Shandong Province. The findings aim to provide standardized technical references for practitioners and extension workers.

---

 2. Core Key Cultivation Technologies
 2.1 Pre-Planting Preparation, Cultivar Screening and Grafting
 2.1.1 Cultivar and rootstock selection
Cultivars are selected according to cropping season and market demand. For winter-spring cropping in solar greenhouses, cultivars with strong chilling tolerance, weak-light tolerance, high parthenocarpy rate and resistance to downy mildew and powdery mildew are preferred (e.g., North China spiny-type cucumbers or mini fruit cucumbers). For autumn-winter cropping, cultivars with high heat tolerance at seedling stage and storage tolerance are selected.
Grafting is a core technical measure to alleviate continuous cropping obstacles and improve stress resistance. Fig-leaf gourd (*Cucurbita ficifolia* Bouché) is used as the dominant rootstock for its high compatibility with cucumber, strong low-temperature tolerance and effective resistance to Fusarium wilt. The top-hole cut-grafting method is recommended, with a survival rate of over 92% under standardized heat and moisture preservation management.
 2.1.2 Site preparation and planting
For soil cultivation, plots are subjected to 20–30 days of solar disinfection with plastic film covering before planting, or treated with dazomet to kill soil-borne pathogens. Decomposed farmyard manure (45–60 t ha⁻¹) and microbial inoculants are applied as basal fertilizer, followed by high-ridging with wide-narrow row spacing (120 cm for wide rows, 60 cm for narrow rows, 25–30 cm ridge height). Drip irrigation pipes are laid under black plastic film to reduce evaporation and air humidity. Grafted seedlings with 3–4 true leaves are planted at a density of 37,500–45,000 plants ha⁻¹ on sunny days. For plots with severe continuous cropping obstacles, soilless cultivation with coconut coir-peat-perlite mixed substrate is recommended to isolate soil-borne pathogens.

 2.2 Precision Multi-Factor Environmental Regulation
Environmental regulation is the core advantage of protected cultivation, and parameters are adjusted dynamically according to growth stages:
- Temperature management: Four-stage temperature regulation is adopted during the fruiting period to balance photosynthesis and nutrient consumption: 26–30 ℃ from 8:00 to 13:00 to promote photosynthesis; 22–25 ℃ from 13:00 to 18:00; 15–18 ℃ from 18:00 to 24:00 to facilitate assimilate transport; and 11–13 ℃ from 0:00 to 8:00 to reduce respiratory consumption. The minimum night temperature is kept above 10 ℃ to avoid chilling injury.
- Light management: Long-life anti-dripping polyolefin (PO) film with light transmittance above 90% is used for greenhouse covering, and reflective screens are hung on the back wall in winter to increase canopy light intensity. For summer cultivation, 40% shading nets are covered only at noon under high temperature and strong light to avoid sunscald.
- Humidity management: Relative air humidity is controlled at 70–80% during the seedling stage and 60–75% during the fruiting period. Ventilation is carried out gradually after greenhouse temperature rises in the morning to dehumidify without causing sharp temperature drops.
- CO₂ enrichment: On sunny days from December to March, CO₂ fertilizer is applied 0.5–1 hour after thermal insulation covering is removed in the morning, maintaining a CO₂ concentration of 800–1000 μmol mol⁻¹ until 30 minutes before ventilation, which can increase early yield by 15–20% (Li et al., 2023). No fertilization is conducted on cloudy or snowy days.

 2.3 Integrated Water and Fertilizer Management
The system adopts the principle of “small amount, high frequency and precise matching with growth stages” through drip irrigation under film. Soil moisture is monitored with tensiometers, and irrigation is initiated when soil matric potential reaches -20 to -30 kPa.
- At the seedling and vine elongation stages, dominated by vegetative growth, high-nitrogen water-soluble fertilizer (N-P₂O₅-K₂O = 30-10-10) is applied at a low rate to promote root and stem development.
- After entering the fruiting stage, high-potassium fertilizer (N-P₂O₅-K₂O = 15-10-30) is applied every 7–10 days, and the interval is shortened to 3–5 days during the full harvesting period.
- For substrate cultivation, special nutrient solution for cucumber is used, with EC value controlled at 1.8–2.2 mS cm⁻¹ at seedling stage and 2.2–2.8 mS cm⁻¹ at fruiting stage, and pH maintained at 5.5–6.5.
Humic acid and microbial inoculants are applied every 20–30 days to improve rhizosphere microenvironment and alleviate soil salinization. Compared with traditional flood irrigation and broadcast fertilization, the integrated system reduces total water and fertilizer input by more than 30%.

 2.4 Canopy Adjustment and Harvest Management
For cultivars with dominant main-vine fruiting, all lateral branches and tendrils are removed in time to reduce redundant nutrient consumption. When plants grow to 50–60 cm tall, vines are hung with nylon ropes to keep the canopy upright. Vine lowering is conducted on sunny afternoons (when stems are flexible and not easy to break) after the first batch of fruits is harvested, and 15–20 healthy functional leaves are retained per plant to ensure photosynthetic area. Senescent leaves, diseased leaves and malformed young fruits are removed regularly to improve ventilation and light transmission.
The first root fruit is harvested early (when the fruit reaches commodity length) to avoid inhibiting vegetative growth (“fruit holding back seedling”). During the full fruiting period, fruits are harvested every 2–3 days in the morning to maintain fruit freshness.

 2.5 Green Prevention and Control of Pests and Diseases
The integrated pest management (IPM) strategy prioritizes agricultural, physical and biological control, with chemical control as a supplementary measure, strictly following the pre-harvest interval (PHI) regulation.
- Agricultural control: Adopt resistant cultivars and grafted seedlings, remove crop residues after harvest, and implement crop rotation with Allium crops or legumes to reduce pathogen and pest bases.
- Physical control: 40–50 mesh insect-proof nets are installed at all ventilation openings; yellow sticky traps (300–375 traps ha⁻¹) are hung to trap whiteflies and aphids, and blue traps for leafminers; frequency-vibration insecticidal lamps are equipped for nocturnal pests.
- Biological control: *Encarsia formosa* is released to control *Bemisia tabaci*; *Bacillus subtilis*, *Trichoderma harzianum* and other biocontrol agents are applied through root irrigation or foliar spraying to prevent gray mold, powdery mildew and soil-borne diseases.
- Chemical control: Low-toxicity, low-residue pesticides are selected only when pest/disease thresholds are exceeded, and pesticides with different action mechanisms are rotated to delay resistance. For main diseases including downy mildew (*Pseudoperonospora cubensis*) and gray mold (*Botrytis cinerea*), fungicides are applied mainly before onset or at the early stage.

---

 3. Verification of Application Effects
A two-year (2022–2023) comparative field trial was conducted in a solar greenhouse in Shouguang City, Shandong Province, during the winter-spring cropping cycle. The conventional local farmer practice (flood irrigation,经验-based fertilization, routine chemical pesticide control) was set as the control, and the integrated key technical system described above was set as the treatment. A randomized complete block design with three replications was adopted, with each plot covering 60 m².
Yield, fruit commodity quality, agricultural input and net return were recorded across the whole growth cycle. As shown in Table 1, the integrated technical system significantly outperformed conventional practice in all production and economic indicators. The yield increase mainly derived from reduced flower and fruit abscission under suitable light, temperature and nutrient supply, while the higher premium fruit rate was attributed to lower malformation rate and disease spot rate. Reduced pesticide and fertilizer inputs not only lowered production costs, but also met the requirements of green vegetable production.

Table 1. Production performance of conventional practice and integrated key technology system
| Indicator | Conventional practice | Integrated technology | Change rate (%) |
|----------------------------------------------------------|------------------------|-----------------------|-----------------|
| Total yield (t ha⁻¹)                                     | 85.2 ± 3.1 a           | 104.3 ± 2.7 b         | +22.4           |
| Premium fruit rate (%)                                   | 71.6 ± 2.2 a           | 87.9 ± 1.8 b          | +22.8           |
| Pesticide active ingredient input (kg ha⁻¹)              | 4.2 ± 0.3 a            | 2.5 ± 0.2 b           | -40.5           |
| Irrigation water input (m³ ha⁻¹)                         | 4200 ± 120 a           | 2730 ± 90 b           | -35.0           |
| Chemical fertilizer input (N+P₂O₅+K₂O, kg ha⁻¹)          | 580 ± 25 a             | 394 ± 18 b            | -32.1           |
| Net return (×10³ USD ha⁻¹)                               | 24.8 ± 0.9 a           | 32.5 ± 0.7 b          | +31.0           |

*Note: Values are means ± standard deviation (n=3). Different lowercase letters in the same row indicate significant differences at P<0.05 by Duncan’s multiple range test.*

---

 4. Conclusions and Prospects
High-efficiency protected cucumber production relies on the synergistic matching of multiple technical links rather than a single measure. The key technical system constructed in this study, covering pre-planting grafting and preparation, precision environmental regulation, integrated water-fertilizer supply, scientific canopy management and green pest control, is highly adaptable to Chinese solar greenhouses and plastic high tunnels. It can simultaneously achieve yield improvement, quality upgrading, agricultural input reduction and income increase, and is suitable for large-scale extension in temperate protected vegetable production areas.
Future optimization of the system can be combined with Internet of Things (IoT) real-time monitoring, artificial intelligence decision-making and low-carbon energy supplementary lighting to further reduce labor input and improve the accuracy of environmental and nutrient regulation, supporting the sustainable development of the protected vegetable industry.
